jsnvu6-e146938-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 3, stating the question to be treated—whether Christians are bound to obey secular princes—and cross-referencing the parallel treatment in Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q.10, a.10.
concepts: obedience to secular authority
cross-reference to Aquinas ST II-II q.10 a.10

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e124.summary: Opens the question: whether Christians are bound to obey secular princes.
concepts: framing of the question

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e133.summary: First objection: James 1 calls the evangelical law 'the law of perfect liberty,' which would not be so unless it freed believers from obedience to any secular prince; therefore Christians are not bound to obey secular princes.
claims: James 1 calls the Gospel law the 'law of perfect liberty'
This title implies freedom from obedience to any secular prince
Therefore Christians are not bound to obey secular princes
concepts: James 1 on the 'law of perfect liberty'
evangelical liberty versus civil obedience

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e137.summary: Second objection: anyone may licitly resort to the judgment of one to whom he is bound to obey; but Christians may not licitly resort to the judgment of secular princes, especially unbelieving ones—hence Paul (1 Corinthians 6) rebukes some who resorted to unbelieving secular judges; therefore Christians are not bound to obey secular princes, especially unbelieving ones.
claims: One may licitly resort to the judgment of whomever one is bound to obey
Christians may not licitly resort to the judgment of unbelieving secular judges, per Paul's rebuke in 1 Corinthians 6
Therefore Christians are not bound to obey secular princes, especially unbelieving ones
concepts: 1 Corinthians 6 on resorting to unbelieving judges
obedience inferred from licit resort to judgment

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e156.summary: Sed contra: Romans 13 states that every soul must be subject to the higher powers, and that this concerns secular power is clear from what follows ('it does not bear the sword without cause'); Paul is certainly writing to Christians; therefore Christians are bound to obey secular power.
claims: Romans 13 commands every soul to be subject to the higher powers, and the sword-bearing clause shows this means secular power
Paul addresses this to Christians
Therefore Christians are bound to obey secular power
concepts: Romans 13 on subjection to higher powers

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e174.summary: Opens the responsio: secular princes are either believers or unbelievers, and the question will be resolved in both cases by one self-evident general principle: if a Christian is legitimately subject to secular power, he is bound to obey it in matters within its scope, not merely from fear of punishment but for conscience's sake, since not obeying resists God's ordinance (Romans 13). The response will first show that Christians are legitimately subject to believing secular power, then inquire whether they are legitimately subject to unbelieving secular power.
claims: A general principle governs both cases: legitimate subjection to secular power entails an obligation to obey it in matters within its scope, binding in conscience, not merely from fear
The response divides into treating believing secular power first, then unbelieving secular power
concepts: general principle of obedience binding in conscience
division of the response by believer/unbeliever ruler

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e200.summary: Proves the first point (legitimacy of believing secular power) in two ways. First: what accords with the dictate of right reason is not removed by faith and grace, since these perfect rather than remove nature and natural reason; but secular prelacy ought to exist among humans according to right reason, as shown in the preceding question; therefore it is not removed from Christians by faith and grace. Second: wherever the order of justice can be disturbed, it is fitting that some hold office to preserve that order; among Christians the order of justice can be disturbed not only spiritually but temporally; therefore it is fitting that some hold office to preserve it temporally too—and only one who presides holds this office (citing Romans 13's exhortation to do good and fear the sword-bearing minister of God). Hence it is fitting, by right reason, that among Christians some preside not only spiritually (ecclesiastical prelates) but also temporally (secular princes); so secular power among Christians is legitimate, and subjects are bound to obey it in matters pertaining to its right.
claims: Faith and grace perfect rather than remove what right reason requires, and right reason requires secular prelacy; hence secular prelacy is not removed from Christians
The order of justice can be disturbed among Christians in temporal as well as spiritual matters, requiring an office—secular princely authority—to preserve it
Secular power among Christians is therefore legitimate, and subjects owe it obedience within its proper scope
concepts: faith and grace as perfecting nature, not destroying it
necessity of an office to preserve temporal justice
legitimacy of believing secular authority

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e248.summary: Turns to the second point: whether an unbelieving secular prince can rightly rule believing Christians, and whether they must obey him. Distinguishes: the unbeliever's dominion over the Christian either pre-exists their distinction by faith and unbelief (as when a subject or servant converts but the ruler does not, common in the early Church and still occurring with servants of Jews), or is newly introduced. In the first case, some hold that the believer/unbeliever distinction does not ipso facto remove the preceding dominion, since divine right (from grace) does not remove human right (from natural reason), and prelacy rests on natural/human right while the believer/unbeliever distinction is from divine right—so believing subjects remain bound to obey unbelieving rulers. They add, however, that such dominion, though not removed automatically, can be justly removed by the Church's ordination (which has God's authority), since unbelievers by their unbelief deserve to lose power over believers—something the Church sometimes does and sometimes does not. Where unbelievers are themselves temporally subject to the Church or its members, the Church has established that a Jewish master's servant, upon becoming Christian, is freed at once if born into servitude or purchased for servitude, or (if purchased for trade) must be offered for sale within three months (citing canon law); this is no injury to the Jews, since as servants of the Church it may dispose of their property, just as secular princes issue laws favoring liberty. Where unbelievers are not so subject, the Church has not established this right, though it justly could, in order to avoid scandal—just as Christ (Matthew 17) could have excused himself from tribute but paid it to avoid scandal.
claims: Where an unbeliever's dominion over a now-Christian subject pre-exists their religious distinction, it is not automatically dissolved, since human right (grounding prelacy) is not overridden by divine right (grounding the believer/unbeliever distinction) alone
Such dominion can nonetheless be justly removed by ecclesiastical authority, since unbelief can merit loss of power over believers

The Church has exercised this authority for unbelievers already subject to it (e.g., Jewish masters of Christian servants) but not, to preserve peace and avoid scandal, for unbelievers outside its jurisdiction
concepts: human right versus divine right
ecclesiastical authority to dissolve unbelievers' dominion
avoidance of scandal as a limiting principle
canon law on Jewish ownership of Christian servants

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e341.summary: States the author's own position: the first point (pre-existing dominion is not ipso facto dissolved by conversion) is true absolutely. The addendum (that it can be justly dissolved by ecclesiastical authority, since unbelief can merit loss of power over believers) is also true, but requires an added qualification: such dominion is ipso facto lost, or at least can be justly taken away by the Church, only if the unbelieving ruler, not content with his legitimate authority, actively strives to draw the converted subject or servant back to unbelief, or disturbs him through insults to the Creator, rather than letting him remain undisturbed as before.
claims: Pre-existing dominion of an unbeliever over a convert is not automatically dissolved by the convert's baptism
The Church can justly dissolve it, but only when the unbelieving ruler actively tries to reconvert or disturbs the convert through insults to God—not merely by virtue of his own continuing unbelief
concepts: qualification distinguishing active hostility from mere unbelief
authorial position (recitative disputation)

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e372.summary: Proves this qualification by reason and by analogy. Reason: a lesser lord who procures and persuades departure from the higher lord from whom he derives all his authority to rule is thereby deprived, or justly deserves to be deprived, of his own authority; an unbelieving ruler who strives to draw a converted subject back to unbelief, blaspheming the Creator, does exactly this—persuading departure from God, the source of all power (Romans 13)—and so justly deserves to lose his authority. Analogy: the mutual obligation of spouses is as great as that of subject to prince or servant to lord; if one spouse converts and the unbelieving spouse will not remain together except by drawing the believer back to unbelief or through blasphemy, the believer is released from the marriage bond; likewise an unbelieving ruler who tries to reconvert a Christian subject through blasphemy deserves to lose his right of lordship—on which basis Christians justly wage war, by the Church's authority, against unbelievers who impede the faith through blasphemy, evil persuasion, or open persecution; and this condition is presumed fulfilled for Saracen or Jewish rulers generally, given their probable and experientially confirmed obstinate hostility to converts.
claims: A lesser lord who persuades departure from his own superior forfeits his derived authority; an unbelieving ruler who tries to draw a convert back to unbelief does the analogous thing with respect to God, the source of all power, and so forfeits his authority
The Pauline privilege in marriage (release from the bond when an unbeliever will not cohabit peaceably) parallels and supports the same conclusion for political dominion
This condition (active hostility to the convert) is presumed fulfilled for Saracen and Jewish rulers generally, based on probable and repeated experience of their obstinate opposition to converts
concepts: derived authority forfeited by rebellion against its source
analogy to the Pauline privilege in marriage
presumption of hostility toward converts among Saracen and Jewish rulers
just war for the Church's protection of converts

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e441.summary: Considers the converse case: if the unbelieving ruler is content with his legitimate authority, does not try to reconvert the subject, does not blaspheme the Creator, and lets the subject remain undisturbed, it is not evident that he should justly lose his authority—since the subject's new conversion, without any new sin by the ruler, is the subject's merit, not the ruler's fault, so the ruler's unchanged unbelief cannot suffice to forfeit dominion he already held legitimately. If there is any ground for release, it would have to come from the convert's own merit; yet although the convert merits something far greater than civil liberty (freedom from sin, eternal life), this does not entail meriting release from a subjection that in no way prejudices the faith. Moreover, the Church's God-given authority does not exceed the limits of Scripture, and Scripture expressly commands converts to remain subject to their former (even unbelieving) lords and to obey them—citing Romans 13 (princes as ministers of God, owed tribute), 1 Peter 2 (subjection to the king and governors, even unbelieving, as God's will), and 1 Timothy 6 (servants under the yoke to honor their—unbelieving—masters). Scripture thus does not suggest, and rather suggests the opposite, that conversion alone merits release from an unbelieving master's power.
claims: A benign unbelieving ruler's unchanged unbelief, without active hostility, is not sufficient ground for forfeiting his legitimate authority, since the subject's conversion is not the ruler's fault
Conversion to the faith merits eternal goods but does not thereby merit release from a subjection that does not prejudice the faith itself
Scripture (Romans 13, 1 Peter 2, 1 Timothy 6) expressly commands converts to remain obedient to their former lords, even unbelieving ones, and the Church's authority cannot exceed Scripture's limits
concepts: merit of the convert versus fault of the ruler
limits of ecclesiastical authority relative to Scripture
scriptural texts commanding obedience to unbelieving masters

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e548.summary: Offers a second argument for the same conclusion: it is illicit to compel to the faith unbelievers who have never received it; but if the Church deprived an unbelieving ruler of his right over converted subjects, it would thereby compel unconverted subjects and servants to the faith through fear of losing their master's goods and position, since a servant is his lord's property and every subject is bound to his lord in some way; but no power extends to what is illicit; therefore the Church cannot generally deprive an otherwise-benign unbelieving ruler of his authority over converts.
claims: Depriving an unbelieving ruler of authority over converts would create an illicit inducement (fear of loss) compelling his other subjects toward conversion
Since no power extends to illicit acts, the Church cannot generally exercise such deprivation absent the ruler's active hostility
concepts: prohibition on compelling conversion
servant as property implicated in the ruler's incentive structure

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e572.summary: Offers a third argument, again by analogy to marriage: if one spouse converts and the unbeliever consents to cohabit without drawing the believer to unbelief or blaspheming the Creator, the marriage bond is not, and should not be, dissolved; likewise, if an unbelieving ruler or lord demands from a converted subject or servant only what pertains to his rightful lordship, without trying to draw him back to unbelief or disturbing him through blasphemy, the prior obligation of servant to lord or subject to prince is not, and cannot justly be, dissolved. Notes, however, that as said before, this benign condition perhaps does not now hold, and has long not held, given unbelievers' obstinate hostility—for which reason a converted spouse is forbidden to cohabit with an unbelieving one (per canon law), and this benign condition is now presumed unfulfilled; hence the doctors say a converted servant or subject can be absolved by the Church from an unbelieving ruler's dominion—though the author judges this conclusion rests on the presumed failure of the benign condition, not on unbelief alone. This concludes the treatment of obedience owed to unbelieving lords when dominion pre-exists the believer/unbeliever distinction.
claims: By analogy with the marriage case, a benign unbelieving ruler's dominion over a peaceable convert is not dissolved, in principle

In practice, this benign condition is presumed not to hold given unbelievers' habitual hostility, which is why the doctors permit the Church to absolve converts from unbelieving rulers' dominion—but this rests on the presumed factual failure of the condition, not on a general right independent of it
concepts: marriage analogy applied a third time
presumption against the benign-unbeliever condition in practice
author's qualification of the doctors' common view

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e631.summary: Treats the case of newly-introduced prelacy of unbelievers over believers: the Church in no way permits unbelievers to acquire dominion over believers or to be placed in office over them, reasonably so, since this risks scandal and danger to the faith—those subject to another's jurisdiction are easily influenced by it (as many passages in the Books of Kings show), and unbelievers despise the faith upon perceiving believers' defects. Where such dominion has nevertheless been introduced (as when some Christian princes make certain Jews provosts or bailiffs), those responsible sin by acting against the Church's statute; nonetheless subjects remain bound to obey the Jews so instituted in matters pertaining to the just execution of the office entrusted to them.
claims: The Church categorically forbids newly introducing unbelievers' dominion or office over believers, due to the risk of scandal and erosion of faith through influence and contempt
Where such introduction occurs despite the prohibition, those responsible sin, but subjects must still obey the unbeliever in matters pertaining to the just execution of his office
concepts: prohibition on newly introducing unbelievers' authority over believers
risk of scandal and doctrinal erosion
obligation to obey even an illicitly-instituted officeholder within his proper function

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e664.summary: Reply to the first opposing argument (d1e133): the evangelical law is called the law of perfect liberty because it frees from the servitude of sin (the worst servitude) and from the entire old law, which scarcely anyone could ever fully bear—not because it frees from civil servitude, by which a subject is bound to obey his lord, since such obedience is consonant with reason and meritorious.
claims: 'Perfect liberty' in James 1 refers to freedom from sin and from the old law, not from civil obedience, which remains reasonable and meritorious
concepts: reply to objection
clarification of evangelical liberty

jsnvu6-e146938-d1e682.summary: Reply to the second opposing argument (d1e137): the major premise is false. Obeying a prince in matters pertaining to his dominion is a matter of necessity, whereas voluntarily bringing another to judgment before an unbelieving judge is a matter of choice; hence the first is owed, the second is not but is purely optional—so where it tends toward danger it is illicit, which is the case Paul addresses. As for Christ's statement (Matthew 17) that 'the sons are free,' he speaks of himself as Son of the eternal King (per Peter's confession at Matthew 16), and so was free from the debt of tribute—unlike us, and unlike the other believers of that time, whom the Lord commanded to pay tribute to the unbelieving prince (Matthew 22: 'Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's').
claims: The objection's major premise is false: obedience within a lord's proper dominion is necessary and owed, while resorting to judgment before an unbelieving judge is merely voluntary and licit only when not dangerous
Christ's claim to be free from tribute (Matthew 17) concerns his unique divine sonship, not a general exemption of believers, who are instead commanded (Matthew 22) to render Caesar his due
concepts: reply to objection
necessary versus voluntary obligations
Christ's unique filial exemption distinguished from the general Christian duty

jsnvu6-e146938.summary: Question 3 asks whether Christians are bound to obey secular princes. Objections argue from the Gospel's status as 'the law of perfect liberty' and from Paul's rebuke of Christians who resorted to unbelieving judges (1 Corinthians 6) that Christians are exempt from obedience to secular rulers; the sed contra invokes Romans 13's command of subjection to the higher powers. The responsio establishes a general principle—legitimate subjection to secular power binds obedience in conscience, not merely from fear—and applies it first to believing rulers (whose legitimacy follows from right reason's requirement of an office to preserve temporal justice, which faith and grace perfect rather than abolish) and then, at length, to unbelieving rulers. For pre-existing dominion of an unbeliever over a subject who converts, the text distinguishes: such dominion is not automatically dissolved by conversion, since human right (grounding prelacy) is not simply overridden by the believer/unbeliever distinction (grounded in divine right); but it can be justly dissolved by the Church when the unbelieving ruler actively tries to draw the convert back to unbelief or blasphemes the Creator (paralleled to a lesser lord's forfeiture for persuading revolt against his superior, and to the Pauline privilege in marriage)—whereas a benign, non-hostile unbelieving ruler retains his authority, since Scripture commands obedience even to unbelieving masters and the Church's authority cannot exceed Scripture's limits. In practice, however, the benign condition is presumed unfulfilled given unbelievers' habitual hostility to converts, which is why the Church in practice often does permit release. Newly-introduced dominion of unbelievers over believers, by contrast, is categorically forbidden by the Church to avoid scandal, though subjects must still obey an unbeliever illicitly placed in office within the bounds of that office. The replies to the opening objections clarify that evangelical liberty concerns freedom from sin and the old law, not civil obedience, and that necessary obedience to a lord's rightful dominion differs from the merely voluntary act of resorting to judgment before an unbelieving judge.
claims: Christians are bound in conscience to obey secular power, believing or unbelieving, insofar as it operates within its legitimate scope, since such authority is required by right reason (which faith perfects rather than abolishes) and is affirmed by Scripture (Romans 13, 1 Peter 2, 1 Timothy 6)

Pre-existing dominion of an unbeliever over a convert is not automatically dissolved by the convert's baptism, but can be justly removed by the Church specifically when the ruler actively opposes the convert's faith, not merely by virtue of his own unbelief

The Church categorically forbids newly instituting unbelievers' authority over believers, due to the risk of scandal and doctrinal erosion, though obedience is still owed within such an office if it is nonetheless established
Evangelical liberty concerns freedom from sin and the old law, not exemption from civil obedience, which remains reasonable and meritorious
concepts: obedience to secular authority (believing and unbelieving)
human right versus divine right
ecclesiastical authority to dissolve dominion, and its limits under Scripture
presumption of unbelievers' hostility to converts
prohibition on newly introduced dominion of unbelievers over believers
